concepts.name: Rayleigh scattering
concepts.definition: Scattering of light by particles much smaller than its wavelength; intensity scales as 1/λ⁴.
concepts.realWorldExample: Air molecules scatter blue (~450nm) about 5.5x more than red (~700nm).

concepts.name: Wavelength
concepts.definition: The distance between successive wave crests; visible light spans roughly 380–750 nanometers.

concepts.name: Sunset reddening
concepts.definition: At low sun angles light crosses ~40x more atmosphere, so most blue is scattered away before reaching your eye.

concepts.name: Optical path length
concepts.definition: The distance light travels through a medium; longer paths mean more scattering events.

concepts.name: Mie scattering
concepts.definition: Scattering by particles comparable to the wavelength (droplets, dust); nearly wavelength-independent, which is why clouds are white.

keyFacts.title: Blue scatters ~5.5x more than red
keyFacts.detail: Follows directly from the 1/λ⁴ law with 450nm vs 700nm light.

keyFacts.title: Sunset light crosses ~40x more air
keyFacts.detail: Low-angle geometry multiplies the optical path through the atmosphere.

keyFacts.title: The sky isn't violet because of your eyes
keyFacts.detail: Violet scatters even more than blue, but solar output and cone sensitivity favor blue.

keyFacts.title: Clouds are white due to Mie scattering
keyFacts.detail: Droplets scatter all visible wavelengths nearly equally.

experiments.title: Build the tank sky
experiments.instruction: Fill a clear rectangular tank with water and stir in a few drops of milk until faintly cloudy.
experiments.expectedResult: The water looks faintly bluish from the side.

experiments.title: Make a sunset
experiments.instruction: Shine the flashlight through the long axis and view the beam end-on from the far side.
experiments.expectedResult: The transmitted beam looks orange — the milk particles scattered the blue away.

experiments.title: Overdo it
experiments.instruction: Keep adding milk and watch the beam whiten as particle sizes push into the Mie regime.
experiments.expectedResult: The blue tint disappears; scattering becomes wavelength-independent.
experiments.safetyNote: None — but the milk-water does not keep; pour it out after.

quiz.question: How does Rayleigh scattering intensity depend on wavelength?
quiz.explanation: The inverse fourth-power law is why short (blue) wavelengths dominate the scattered sky.

quiz.question: Why are clouds white rather than blue?
options: Droplets are large enough for Mie scattering, which is wavelength-independent
Clouds reflect the sun's surface color
quiz.explanation: Droplets are comparable to or larger than visible wavelengths, so all colors scatter equally.

quiz.question: Why isn't the sky violet, even though violet scatters most?
options: There is no violet in sunlight
Solar output and human cone sensitivity both favor blue
Violet light is too fast to scatter
quiz.explanation: Less violet arrives from the sun and our eyes respond to it weakly.

synthesis_response.tldr: Air molecules scatter short wavelengths ~5.5x more than red (1/λ⁴), painting the sky blue by day and red at sunset — and you can recreate both in a fish tank.
keyTakeaways: Rayleigh scattering scales as 1/λ⁴ — blue dominates the scattered light
Sunsets are red because low-angle light crosses ~40x more atmosphere
Clouds are white because droplet-sized particles scatter all colors equally (Mie)
synthesis_response.masterSummary: An explainer building from wavelength basics to Rayleigh's 1/λ⁴ law, using it to explain the blue sky, red sunsets via optical path length, and white clouds via Mie scattering — capped by a three-step milk-and-flashlight tank experiment that recreates each regime.
